On Mars: Exploration of the Red Planet 1958-1978 (NASA SP-4212)

Mariner 4 did what no machine had done: it photographed another planet. Small and spare, built to fly past Mars once and send home whatever it could in the hours it had, it carried a camera and a tape recorder across the solar system and in July 1965 returned the first close-up pictures ever taken of another world — 22 grainy frames of a cratered, moon-like surface. Those images ended a century of speculation about Martian canals and civilisations in a single afternoon, and proved a spacecraft could cross interplanetary space and bring back a planet’s face. Every camera humanity has since sent to another world descends from this one.
The first successful Mars flyby — July 1965. The 22 grainy black-and-white photos returned ended over a century of speculation about Martian canals and life by showing a cratered, Moon-like surface.
First spacecraft to reach Mars and return close-up images of another planet
First US lunar orbiter (1966-08-14); mapped Apollo landing sites and took the first photo of Earth from lunar orbit (1966).
Second US lunar orbiter (1966-11-10). Took the 'Picture of the Century' — oblique view of Copernicus crater at ~45 km altitude
Third US lunar orbiter (1967-02-08). Photographed Surveyor 1 sitting on the lunar surface — first photo of a spacecraft on another world
Fourth US lunar orbiter (1967-05-08). First polar lunar orbit; mapped 99 % of the near side at 60 m/pixel + far-side regions
Final US lunar orbiter (1967-08-05). Completed far-side mapping at 60 m/pixel; impacted 1968-01-31 ahead of Apollo lunar operations
First spacecraft to orbit another planet
